candidates.title: Smundar: End-to-End Demo | Governed Data Access for AI Agents
candidates.description:
Smundar is a governed semantic data platform designed to give AI agents controlled access to enterprise data without exposing database credentials or allowing LLMs to generate and execute arbitrary SQL.

Instead of relying on unrestricted LLM-generated queries, Smundar uses human-approved semantic mappings and deterministic execution to keep data access bounded, explainable, and auditable.

In this end-to-end demo, I walk through the complete workflow using a sample database, including:

• Connecting a data source
• Discovering datasets
• Querying data using natural language
• Literal overrides and semantic mappings
• Building reusable semantic memory
• Execution logs and auditability
• Connecting AI agents through MCP

Smundar currently supports major enterprise data platforms including SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Databricks, Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Oracle, and ClickHouse.

Learn more: https://smundar.com

candidates.title: How a $5,000 Test Exposed a Broken B2B Playbook
candidates.description:
Chris told a story that I keep coming thinking about:

He's at a medical device company spending $37 million a year on sales and $2.5 million on marketing, most of that going to headcount and events. He asks to test a different approach. They give him $5,000.

For context, customer acquisition cost was around $100,000. A $5,000 dollar budget shouldn't be able to prove anything. You'd need twenty times that to buy one customer.

It landed three.

So he takes the numbers to the CEO. Pipeline velocity, acquisition cost, growth rate, all pointing the same direction.

They shut the program down. Doubled the sales headcount the next year instead.

He left, brought the same strategy to another company, and watched the exact same thing happen nine months later.

That's the part that stuck with me. One shutdown is a bad call. Two is a pattern. And the pattern isn't that leaders can't read data. It's that nobody gets fired for doubling the sales team.

And I don't think it's a 2015 story. I still watch it happen. Marketing outperforms, the CEO likes the number, then goes and hires more salespeople. The data was never the problem.

candidates.title: Go-to-Market Without a Category: How Iprova Sold to Sony and Philips
candidates.description:
Julian Nolan quit a senior corporate job at Honeywell to build a company that uses Artificial Intelligence to invent — actual, patentable, commercially valuable inventions — for companies like Philips, Sony, Procter & Gamble and Beiersdorf. Fifteen years later, more than 1,500 granted patents have come out of Iprova's tools, and Philips is still a customer. Anastasia Albert, founder of B2B Practitioners, sat down with Julian, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Iprova, together with Norman Rohr, Partner at B2B Practitioners and Chief Executive Officer at Finway, who has advised Julian on Go-to-Market since they met at a business plan competition in 2008. This one is for anyone selling something the market doesn't have a category for yet. We go through all four business models Iprova went through — Intellectual Property investment fund, invention service provider, software plus service, and now self-serve software and why each shift happened. Julian explains the move that made the whole thing work: wrapping a service layer around an unfinished product so he could go to market years earlier than the technology allowed. Norman breaks down the part most founders get wrong — the objections. Plus: how Iprova bootstrapped a deep tech company without venture capital, why founder-led sales stayed the dominant motion far longer than it should have, and how you build trust in a market where every company now claims to be an AI company.

candidates.title: The AEO Playbook: 10 Triggers That Get You Cited by AI
candidates.description:
Most AEO advice optimizes the easy 15% and ignores the 85% that matters. Schema, headings, and front-loading only get you retrieved, not cited. The strongest predictors are mostly earned and off-page: brand authority is the single biggest factor in 2026 research, and 85% of top-funnel B2B AI mentions come from third-party content, not you. So your blog can be perfectly structured and still never get cited — the model has no outside consensus to trust.

In this video: how citation decisions get made, the ten triggers by evidence, and a repeatable monthly audit.

The headline: on-page gets you retrieved, off-page authority gets you cited — and the only proof is querying the engines yourself and tracking citation rate down to the pipeline.

Sources: 2026 studies of millions of AI citations (AirOps, Omniscient, Kevin Indig, Wellows) plus GrowthSpree data. AI citation is probabilistic and varies by engine — directional.

THE FRAMEWORK
Two pathways run in parallel. Parametric presence is off-page — brand mentions, directories, entity records in the model's memory. Retrieval presence is on-page — structure, indexability, extractability. A brand can be strong in one and invisible in the other, and commercial B2B queries (comparisons, shortlists) sit almost entirely in retrieval. Within retrieval, a citation passes four gates — crawled, relevant, trusted, named — and satisfying three still leaves you uncited: off-page authority is what earns the named citation.

THE 10 CITATION TRIGGERS (ranked by evidence)

Brand authority — the strongest single predictor; citations skew high-authority. 2. Third-party mentions — most top-funnel B2B AI mentions come from others' content; they beat backlinks ~3:1. 3. Review/directory presence — a G2, Capterra, or Trustpilot profile ~3x citation odds. 4. Multi-platform presence — sources on 4+ platforms get cited more. 5. Answer-first structure — 44% of citations come from the first 30% of a page; answer in 40-60 words. 6. Comparative listicles — "Best X for Y" is the highest-citing format. 7. Validation content — reviews, listicles, case studies win branded queries; thought leadership rarely does. 8. Clean formatting — consistent headings and extractable chunks get rephrased far more. 9. Original data — engines cite pages that originate a claim, not summaries; publish first-party data. 10. Freshness — updates within three months are cited far more, if substance changed. Most are earned, not on-page tricks.

THE MONTHLY AUDIT
This is the part almost nobody does — why most AEOs fly blind. Monthly, take the 20-30 questions your buyers actually ask and run them across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Gemini, and Google AI Overviews. Log everything: direct citations, unlinked mentions, competitor wins, and ghost citations — you shaped the answer, someone else got the link. Track citation rate, not rankings — engines cite you or skip you. Measure each engine separately; overlap is low, so a gap on one hides on another. Separate being mentioned from memory from being cited from a retrieved page — different fixes. And it's probabilistic: no audit predicts whether an engine cites you on a given day. Then act: strengthen the third-party pages already cited for you, and fix the triggers where competitors win.

candidates.title: Drivers of Enterprise AI Success: Context, Control & Collaboration
candidates.description:
In this episode on Enterprise Unlocked, Thomas Scott, CEO of Wrike, joins the Enterprise Talk bureau to discuss how hands-on leadership and full-stack professionals can drive enterprise AI returns. 

Tom emphasizes the importance of an approach rooted in the three C’s: Context, Control, and Collaboration. He describes ‘integrated non-conformists’ as successful leaders and professionals in this context, aiming for transformation while remaining strongly rooted in the enterprise community. 

The highlight of this conversation was the emphasis on a human-centric approach to realistic AI success, with gradual transformation, people engagement, and fundamental process redesign taking center stage. 

“I am human-centric first and foremost. I've spent my career in technology, but it's building technology for humans. What gets me excited about this era is that the full-stack model of employee development unlocks the potential for broad creativity and application.”

~ Thomas Scott, CEO at Wrike

Key Questions Answered: 
• What are the main reasons for enterprises getting less than stellar results from AI adoption?
• What are the major friction points in AI adoption? 
• What are the different approaches being adopted to transition to AI-powered workflows that you've seen?
• How does a full-stack professional work in practice, and how are you seeing that play out in different departments?
• How hands-on does leadership need to be in heading this change and leading the path forward?
• What's the role of imagination and creativity in all of this, and how can we get the best out of AI?
• What are some strategies and frameworks to make an enterprise's data AI-ready? 
• How do you see enterprise AI shaping up in the next three years or five years or so? 

Key Themes and Takeaways From the Conversation:

1. The Three Forces of AI Adoption: People, Process, and Technology

• Many enterprises focus on the technology while neglecting process redesign and people engagement.
• Automating a flawed or overly complex process scales inefficiency and generates organizational friction.

2. The Shift to "Full-Stack Professionals"

• Enterprise workflows are shifting toward "full-stack professionals" who combine deep expertise in one area with broad cross-functional understanding.
• Career advancement now favors curious, adaptable, and "always learning" mindsets.

3. Non-Negotiable "Hands-On" Leadership

• Leaders must actively use their company's tools and directly feel operational friction points.
• A leader’s responsibility is to set aggressive goals, remain realistic about friction, enable teams, and celebrate wins.

4. Process Redesign: Linear vs. Orchestrated Parallel Workflows

• True efficiency and transformation require a fundamental redesign of processes from sequential handoffs to parallel workflows orchestrated around a common center.
• Redesign isn't an overnight "big bang" flip; it progresses from simple tasks to structural workflow overhauls over time.

5. The "Three Cs" Framework & Human-in-the-Loop

• Context: AI effectiveness relies on contextual datasets that capture relationships, timestamps, and user interactions.
• Control: Strong governance, auditability, access control, and clear accountability are critical.
• Collaboration: AI is meant to augment, not replace human decision-making and creativity.

6. Driving Organizational Change: The "Integrated Non-Conformist"

• When driving enterprise-wide change, simplify the objective down to a shared outcome before adding back technical complexity.
• Enterprise leaders need to identify and empower an Integrated Non-Conformist: a champion who is accepted and respected inside the organizational culture, yet possesses the non-conformist drive required to challenge the status quo and push change forward.

candidates.title: The Future of Work with AI: Moving from Individual Gains to Collective Intelligence, by Jonathan ...
candidates.description:
Abstract: This report synthesizes recent evidence on how artificial intelligence is reshaping work, drawing from Microsoft's 2025 New Future of Work Report and the broader research literature. While 2024 marked individual productivity gains from generative AI, 2025 signals a critical shift toward collective productivity—how teams, organizations, and communities can improve together with AI. Adoption continues to accelerate globally, with enterprise ChatGPT messages increasing eightfold year-over-year, yet organizational success depends heavily on employee engagement, trust, and participatory design rather than top-down mandates. Evidence reveals meaningful productivity gains and time savings, particularly in knowledge work, but also emerging challenges including AI-generated "workslop," cognitive deskilling risks, and mixed labor market effects concentrated among early-career workers. Human-AI collaboration is evolving from passive tool use to active partnership, requiring new interaction paradigms, robust common ground, and cognitively engaging workflows. Teams face distinct challenges as AI shifts from supporting individuals to enabling group work, demanding new evaluation frameworks, proactive agent behaviors, and careful attention to social dynamics. This report examines adoption patterns, workforce impacts, collaboration design, cognitive implications, and sector-specific transformations while highlighting that AI's ultimate value depends not on technical capabilities alone but on intentional organizational choices that prioritize human agency, skill development, and equitable outcomes.
